claims.text: secrets.sgit.ai was created on 5 October as a zero-knowledge secrets manager that runs entirely in the browser, with passkey unlock and ciphertext in a GCP bucket.
claims.quote: was created on 5 October as "A zero-knowledge secrets manager that runs entirely in the browser

claims.text: At v0.1.13 on 6 October its reality page lists 75 claims: 42 shipped, 28 proposed and 5 deliberately absent.
claims.quote: a reality page generated from a list of 75 claims, 42 shipped, 28 proposed and 5 deliberately absent

value.unit: claims shipped on the reality page

claims.text: What is shipped is the site, the release pipeline, the labs and the review tools; the app itself, sign-in, passkey unlock and the keyring, is all proposed.
claims.quote: The app itself, sign-in, passkey unlock, the keyring, is all proposed.

claims.text: Its passkey work went into this newsroom instead, where the passkey opens the vault for every reader.
claims.quote: Its passkey work went into this newsroom instead, where the passkey opens the vault for every reader.

claims.text: The site's sharing scheme already has each browser generate a key pair and publish the public key in a directory: the public key shares keys, not data, and the server can never read the package.
claims.quote: The public key shares keys, not data. The server carries the package and can never read it.

claims.text: The sharing scheme was planned for phase 2; it becomes the product.
claims.quote: It was planned for phase 2. It becomes the product.

claims.text: The sgit team's security review of 6 August found the two-word code path broken and to be treated as compromised for anything sensitive, while the passphrase-vault path is sound.
claims.quote: path is broken and should be treated as compromised for anything sensitive.

claims.text: A two-word token carries 30.2 bits, and its public id is an unsalted hash of it, so anyone who sees the id can recover the token offline.
claims.quote: A token carries 30.2 bits; the public id is an unsalted hash of it

claims.text: Because the key derivation uses one fixed salt, a single precomputed table decrypts every vault ever created with a two-word code.
claims.quote: because the key derivation uses one fixed salt, a single precomputed table decrypts every vault ever created with one.

claims.text: The command line team disabled creating two-word codes in June.
claims.quote: The command line team had already disabled creating them in June.

claims.text: The previous article said the short code was fine for a quick one-time drop; it is not, and that article now says so.
claims.quote: it is not, and that article now says so.

claims.text: The hard part was never the encryption but getting the key to the other side without friction, which is also why SG/Send did not take off.
claims.quote: the hard part was never the encryption, it was getting the key to the other side without friction.

claims.text: Public keys remove the need to move a secret key at all.
claims.quote: Public keys remove the need to move a secret key at all.

claims.text: Ask me for a secret: I send my public key as a link, QR code, email or WhatsApp message, and the secret comes back encrypted to it as a one-time drop, a file or a QR code.
claims.quote: I send my public key, as a link, a QR code, an email or a WhatsApp message.

claims.text: A short secret encrypted with an RSA-4096 key is 512 bytes, well inside one QR code.
claims.quote: a short secret encrypted with an RSA-4096 key is 512 bytes, well inside one QR code.

value.unit: bytes for a short secret under RSA-4096

claims.text: A browser key that cannot be exported survived a full browser restart in the test and still decrypted, while refusing to be exported.
claims.quote: in the test, it survived a full browser restart and still decrypted, while refusing to be exported.

claims.text: With no server at all, sgit pki encrypt produces a file that can travel over any channel; the receiver needs only the private key.
claims.quote: sgit pki encrypt produces a file that can travel over any channel; the receiver needs only the private key.

claims.text: Each person gets an identity vault dedicated to their key pair, encrypted like any other and unlocked by their passkey through the WebAuthn PRF extension.
claims.quote: Each person gets an identity vault, a vault dedicated to their key pair, encrypted like any other, and unlocked by their passkey through the WebAuthn PRF extension

claims.text: The recovery code the secrets site specifies is 26 characters, 128 bits, shown once.
claims.quote: 26 characters, 128 bits, shown once.

claims.text: The password manager keeps the passkey, which it is built for; the private key never goes into it but stays in the vault, and the passkey opens it.
claims.quote: The private key never goes into the password manager; it stays in the vault, and the passkey opens it.

claims.text: PRF was reported working with passkeys in Google Password Manager, iCloud Keychain, Windows Hello and Firefox, and Bitwarden supports PRF-capable passkeys too.
claims.quote: PRF working with passkeys in Google Password Manager, iCloud Keychain, Windows Hello and Firefox, and Bitwarden supports PRF-capable passkeys too.

claims.text: Storing a secret in the browser's own password store through PasswordCredential is not a foundation, because it is not Baseline and does not work in some of the most widely-used browsers.
claims.quote: not Baseline because it does not work in some of the most widely-used browsers

claims.text: Append lanes are already write-only inboxes read with an enum key, and this site has measured a hundred writers on one.
claims.quote: Append lanes are already write-only inboxes, read with an enum key, and this site has measured a hundred writers on one.

value.unit: writers measured on one append lane

claims.text: sgit pki makes RSA-4096 and ECDSA key pairs, encrypts, decrypts and signs, and in the test the agent verified the owner's signature once it knew the owner's key.
claims.quote: sgit pki makes RSA-4096 and ECDSA key pairs, encrypts, decrypts and signs

claims.text: What is missing is the product around the plumbing: a request object carrying a public key and where to write, a signed directory, an envelope format, and a client written here.
claims.quote: a request object that carries a public key and where to write; a signed directory; an envelope format that names the sender, the recipient and the signature

claims.text: The SG/Send web UI became too hard to change, which is why the work paused, so the client is written here rather than there.
claims.quote: the SG/Send web UI, which became too hard to change and is why the work paused.

claims.text: Sending one secret to someone and opening it should be free; it costs almost nothing to serve and it is how people find the service.
claims.quote: Sending one secret to someone and opening it should be free; it costs almost nothing to serve, and it is how people find the service.

claims.text: What is charged for are the capabilities, the identity vault and recovery, the directory, pairing, team inboxes and integrations, even when the bytes do not travel through our servers.
claims.quote: What is charged for are the capabilities: the identity vault and its recovery, the directory and verified fingerprints, pairing new devices and agents, team inboxes and their audit trail, and the integrations.

claims.text: No shared keys, no short codes: every secret is encrypted to a public key and the two-word code is never offered.
claims.quote: No shared keys, no short codes. Every secret is encrypted to a public key; the two-word code is never offered.

claims.text: One format: an envelope with sender, recipient, signature and ciphertext, produced and read by both a JavaScript library and sgit pki.
claims.quote: One format. An envelope with sender, recipient, signature and ciphertext, produced and read by both a JavaScript library and sgit pki.

claims.text: Server changes: request objects and the directory on top of the SG/Send API, and nothing that ever sees a private key.
claims.quote: Server changes. Request objects and the directory on top of the SG/Send API; nothing that ever sees a private key.

claims.text: The service does not exist: secrets.sgit.ai is a site with a design, and the app was never built.
claims.quote: The service does not exist. secrets.sgit.ai is a site with a design; the app was never built.

claims.text: The tests were local: one machine, Chromium, a local SG/Send server, dummy secrets.
claims.quote: The tests were local. One machine, Chromium, a local SG/Send server, dummy secrets.

claims.text: LastPass is unconfirmed: its passkeys exist, and PRF support was not found.
claims.quote: LastPass is unconfirmed. Its passkeys exist; PRF support was not found.

claims.text: The pricing is a proposal; nothing is charged today.
claims.quote: The pricing is a proposal. Nothing is charged today.
